SECTION SUMMARIES:
The book begins with a preface by C. W. C. Oman [PDF p. 11]. He notes that earlier historians viewed Byzantium as decadent [PDF p. 13]. He credits Finlay and Bury with revising this perception [PDF p. 13]. Oman relies on various ancient chroniclers for his research [PDF p. 14].

The first chapter describes the foundation of Byzantium [PDF p. 27]. Megarian colonists founded the city at the Golden Horn [PDF p. 27]. They chose the site following an oracle from Delphi [PDF p. 29]. The location provided a strategic military and commercial advantage [PDF p. 30]. It effectively controlled the trade of the Black Sea [PDF p. 30]. Early records show the city survived Persian and Athenian conflicts [PDF p. 31-32]. Some ancient writers describe the citizens as quite gluttonous [PDF p. 33]. Byzantium later enjoyed status as a free Roman city [PDF p. 34]. The emperor Vespasian later stripped the city of these privileges [PDF p. 34]. In A.D. 196, the city faced destruction under Severus [PDF p. 35]. It later functioned as a vital fortress for Licinius [PDF p. 37]. Constantine eventually won the city in A.D. 323 [PDF p. 38].

The second chapter covers the foundation of Constantinople [PDF p. 39]. Constantine required a more effective administrative and military center [PDF p. 42]. He rejected several sites, including Nicomedia and Ilium [PDF p. 43]. He eventually selected the old Megarian city [PDF p. 43]. Legend suggests he traced the city limits with a spear [PDF p. 44]. The city plan included the seven surrounding hills [PDF p. 44]. The Milion served as a central point for distances [PDF p. 45]. The imperial palace was situated in the south-east [PDF p. 45]. A large forum known as the Augustaeum sat centrally [PDF p. 45]. The Senate House was modeled to resemble the city of Rome [PDF p. 47]. The Patriarch's Palace was located near the imperial residence [PDF p. 47]. This proximity limited the independence of the religious authority [PDF p. 48]. The Hippodrome provided a venue for chariot races [PDF p. 48]. Violent factions like the Blues and Greens emerged there [PDF p. 49]. The central division wall featured a famous Egyptian obelisk [PDF p. 50]. It also held a three-headed brazen serpent [PDF p. 50].

The provided text ends during the description of the Hippodrome [PDF p. 50]. Consequently, the full history of the city remains unresolved [PDF p. 50].

The Hippodrome contained several important monuments [PDF p. 51]. These included a bronze column and a golden tripod [PDF p. 51]. Constantine repurposed a porphyry column with a bronze image [PDF p. 51]. He built an early, basilica-shaped St. Sophia [PDF p. 53]. A wooden gallery connected the church to the palace [PDF p. 53]. Constantine chose Byzantium as his capital in 328 A.D. [PDF p. 54]. The city was consecrated on May 11, 330 A.D. [PDF p. 54]. He attracted diverse populations through privileges and corn distributions [PDF p. 55]. The name New Rome was used mainly in poetry and rhetoric [PDF p. 56].

Constantine died on May 22, 337 A.D. [PDF p. 57]. His successors faced civil wars and barbarian threats [PDF p. 57]. The Goths had settled peacefully near the Danube [PDF p. 60]. However, the Huns attacked the Goths around 372 A.D. [PDF p. 61]. This forced the Visigoths to request entry into Roman territory [PDF p. 62]. Emperor Valens allowed them to settle as subject-allies [PDF p. 63]. Roman officials then extorted food from the starving Goths [PDF p. 63]. Fritigern led a revolt against these corrupt officials [PDF p. 64]. Gothic cavalry proved decisive at the Battle of Adrianople [PDF p. 65, 66]. The resulting defeat decimated the Eastern Roman legions [PDF p. 67].

Theodosius attempted to stabilize the empire through peace treaties [PDF p. 68]. He enlisted Gothic war-bands to serve as imperial auxiliaries [PDF p. 69]. The author argues this experiment was dangerous for the empire [PDF p. 69]. After Theodosius died in 395 A.D., factional wars began [PDF p. 70]. His sons Arcadius and Honorius were both weak rulers [PDF p. 70]. Alaric led the Visigoths into Italy to seek plunder [PDF p. 75]. Meanwhile, the Gothic leader Gainas fell in Constantinople [PDF p. 77]. In 488 A.D., Theodoric conquered Italy for Emperor Zeno [PDF p. 90]. The East survived because of the character of its rulers [PDF p. 86].

Justinus took the throne in 518 A.D. [PDF p. 91]. His nephew, Justinian, became his successor [PDF p. 92]. Justinian married the actress Theodora in 526 A.D. [PDF p. 93]. Theodora was an intelligent and highly influential councillor [PDF p. 94]. Justinian aimed to reconquer the lost Western provinces [PDF p. 99]. He also fought an indecisive war with the Persians [PDF p. 100]. The general Belisarius proved to be a vital asset [PDF p. 100]. Justinian managed a vast revenue through intense taxation [PDF p. 98, 99]. The author compares his greatness to Louis XIV [PDF p. 95].

The text contains legends and several unresolved questions [PDF p. 51, 82]. For example, the cause of Eudocia's exile remains unknown [PDF p. 82]. Some accounts of Theodora's early life may be libellous [PDF p. 93].

The Byzantine factions known as Blues and Greens grew politically powerful [PDF p. 101]. The Blues supported Justinus and maintained strictly orthodox views [PDF p. 101]. Conversely, the Greens supported the late Emperor Anastasius and Monophysitism [PDF p. 101]. In 532, rioting erupted after botched executions of several rioters [PDF p. 102]. This chaos sparked the violent six-day Nika riot [PDF p. 102]. The mob demanded the deposition of John of Cappadocia [PDF p. 102]. They also sought the removal of the prefect Eudemius [PDF p. 102]. Rebels also attempted to install Hypatius as the new Caesar [PDF p. 102-103]. Empress Theodora refused to flee and urged a final assault [PDF p. 105]. Belisarius ultimately routed the rebels in the Hippodrome [PDF p. 105]. This massacre resulted in approximately 35,000 deaths [PDF p. 106].

Justinian later sought to reconquer lost western imperial provinces [PDF p. 107]. Belisarius led an army to defeat the Vandals in 533 [PDF p. 110]. King Gelimer was unable to prevent this swift Vandal defeat [PDF p. 110-111]. Justinian then targeted the Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy [PDF p. 108]. Belisarius seized Sicily and later captured the city of Ravenna [PDF p. 114-117]. The Goths eventually rallied under a king named Baduila [PDF p. 118]. Baduila captured Rome in 550 and ruled for eleven years [PDF p. 120-121]. He was known for his personal courage and sense of justice [PDF p. 120-121]. However, the general Narses defeated the Goths in 553 [PDF p. 121]. This campaign left much of Italy wasted and depopulated [PDF p. 122].

The Persian War forced Justinian to spend immense gold [PDF p. 125]. Simultaneously, a great plague struck the empire in 542 [PDF p. 127]. This pestilence killed 5,000 people every day in Constantinople [PDF p. 127]. The disease spared no race, class, or specific region [PDF p. 128]. Justinian's health and organizational capacity declined after the plague [PDF p. 128]. The death of Theodora in 548 also diminished his energy [PDF p. 129]. He remains significant for his legal codes and architecture [PDF p. 132, 138]. He employed Tribonian to lead a commission for legal codification [PDF p. 138]. He also commissioned the architect Anthemius to rebuild St. Sophia [PDF p. 133].

The successors of Justinian faced increasing chaos and invasions [PDF p. 140]. The Lombards invaded Italy in 568 under King Alboin [PDF p. 141-142]. This migration left many Italian regions under Teutonic control [PDF p. 143]. In the Balkans, the Avars and Slavs attacked the frontiers [PDF p. 148]. The Avars primarily sought plunder through frequent raids [PDF p. 148]. Conversely, the Slavs aimed to establish permanent new homes [PDF p. 148]. These groups occasionally acted separately or in opposition to each other [PDF p. 150]. The papacy also gained power during these turbulent years [PDF p. 145].

Unresolved questions remain regarding the true motives of the factions [PDF p. 101]. The text also notes the unpredictable nature of the plague [PDF p. 128].

The invasion of Slavs and Avars devastated the Latin-speaking Thracian population [PDF p. 151]. This process nearly exterminated the original population north of the Balkan mountains [PDF p. 151]. Contemporary chronicler John of Ephesus described the 581 invasion as very severe [PDF p. 151]. General Priscus struggled to hold the Danube frontier against these nomadic invaders [PDF p. 152]. The inability to stop these incursions contributed to Emperor Maurice's eventual fall [PDF p. 152]. He became unpopular after refusing to pay a large ransom in 599 [PDF p. 152]. In 602, the Danube army revolted and elected Phocas as their emperor [PDF p. 153]. Phocas subsequently executed Maurice and all five of his young sons [PDF p. 153]. The author characterizes Phocas as a brutal and incompetent imperial ruler [PDF p. 154].

Phocas's reign triggered a major war with Chosroes of the Persian Empire [PDF p. 155]. The Persians ravaged North Syria and eventually entered into Asia Minor [PDF p. 155]. In 610, Heraclius overthrew Phocas and claimed the vacant imperial throne [PDF p. 156, 157]. The empire faced chaos and lost Jerusalem to the Persians in 614 [PDF p. 157]. Shahrbarz captured the "True Cross" and carried it into Persia [PDF p. 158]. This loss inspired a new sense of national and religious feeling [PDF p. 159]. Heraclius led several successful campaigns to reclaim these important holy places [PDF p. 161]. He finally secured peace and returned the Holy Wood in 628 [PDF p. 164, 165].

The exhaustion from the Persian war left the empire quite vulnerable [PDF p. 184]. The Saracen invasion then struck the weakened Roman and Persian powers [PDF p. 185]. The Arabs rapidly conquered much of the provinces in Syria and Egypt [PDF p. 189, 190]. During this era, the empire reorganized into military districts called Themes [PDF p. 193, 194]. These units combined military command with provincial and civil administration [PDF p. 195]. Constantine IV successfully defended Constantinople from a massive Arab siege [PDF p. 196, 197]. However, the later reign of Justinian II proved to be very difficult [PDF p. 199]. The author describes him as a selfish and very reckless tyrant [PDF p. 199]. He used extortionate ministers to fund his various unsuccessful wars [PDF p. 200].

The text notes that Syrian conquest details are not well preserved [PDF p. 188]. It also suggests that the origins of the Themes remain puzzling [PDF p. 193].

The era commenced with the usurpation of Leontius in 695 [PDF p. 201]. He overthrew the mutilated Justinian II and ruled for three years [PDF p. 201-202]. Tiberius III subsequently seized the throne with help from Admiral Apsimarus [PDF p. 203]. Justinian II returned to power in 705 with Bulgarian support [PDF p. 205]. His restored reign was defined by extreme vengeance and widespread terror [PDF p. 205-206]. The tyrant was eventually overthrown by Philippicus in 711 [PDF p. 206]. This event initiated years of anarchy under several ephemeral rulers [PDF p. 207]. Leo the Isaurian eventually seized the throne in 717 [PDF p. 209]. He successfully defended Constantinople against a massive Saracen siege [PDF p. 211]. The siege failed due to famine and exceptionally harsh winters [PDF p. 212]. The author attributes the salvation of Christendom to Leo's victory [PDF p. 214].

Leo initiated the Iconoclastic movement to oppose image worship [PDF p. 215]. His son Constantine V intensified these persecutions against the monks [PDF p. 222-223]. He was a true persecutor who used scorpions for punishment [PDF p. 222]. His harsh religious policies earned him the nickname Copronymus [PDF p. 222]. The dynasty continued through Leo IV and the regent Empress Irene [PDF p. 223-224]. Irene blinded her son Constantine VI to maintain her authority [PDF p. 225]. Her reign caused a final breach between Rome and Constantinople [PDF p. 226]. Nicephorus I later took the throne and maintained iconoclast views [PDF p. 229]. Subsequent rulers included Michael I and Leo V, the Chameleon [PDF p. 230-231]. Michael the Amorian ruled after a conspiracy against Leo V [PDF p. 232-233].

Theophilus was a vehement iconoclast who lost the city of Amorium [PDF p. 235-236]. Theodora ended the iconoclastic era by restoring images in 842 [PDF p. 237]. Basil the Macedonian then founded a long and stable dynasty [PDF p. 240]. His successors, Leo VI and Constantine VII, were literary emperors [PDF p. 241]. They focused on writing significant works regarding war and administration [PDF p. 243-246]. The author suggests these men ended a long period of decay [PDF p. 247]. Byzantine art and literature also experienced a significant resurgence [PDF p. 248-250].

The author notes that many details of Leo's reforms remain unknown [PDF p. 220]. Monkish chroniclers often obscured his positive achievements in their writings [PDF p. 220].

The Byzantine Empire derived strength from its monopoly over European commerce [PDF p. 251]. This wealth supported the empire despite its harsh taxation systems [PDF p. 251]. On the eastern frontier, the Caliphate had fractured into several weak states [PDF p. 252]. This fragmentation allowed Nicephorus Phocas to lead successful military campaigns [PDF p. 253]. Phocas conquered Crete in 961 and advanced into Northern Syria [PDF p. 254]. He later became emperor and continued these eastern conquests [PDF p. 256]. Phocas captured many fortresses in Cilicia and North Syria [PDF p. 255]. However, Phocas was unpopular at home due to his fiscal policies [PDF p. 256]. He was eventually murdered by John Zimisces and Theophano in 969 [PDF p. 259].

Zimisces achieved a great victory against the Russians in 971 [PDF p. 261]. He died shortly after his reign, perhaps by poison [PDF p. 265]. Basil II then ruled as a stern and effective emperor [PDF p. 266]. He fought a long war against the Bulgarian King Samuel [PDF p. 267]. Basil achieved a decisive victory and expanded the imperial borders [PDF p. 268]. He died in 1025, leaving the throne to his brother [PDF p. 270]. The Macedonian dynasty eventually ended with the death of Theodora [PDF p. 274].

The extinction of this dynasty triggered civil wars and Seljuk invasions [PDF p. 275]. Constantine Ducas failed to maintain the imperial army's strength [PDF p. 276]. Romanus Diogenes faced the Seljuks but lost at Manzikert in 1071 [PDF p. 280]. He was captured by Alp Arslan and later blinded [PDF p. 281]. Alexius Comnenus eventually restored order through diplomacy and warfare [PDF p. 283]. He fought the Normans and negotiated with the first Crusaders [PDF p. 285-289]. While the Crusades pushed back the Turks, they harmed commerce [PDF p. 292-293]. The Italians gained privileges that depleted the imperial treasury [PDF p. 294]. These privileges included free access to most Byzantine ports [PDF p. 294].

John II ruled with honesty and expanded the eastern frontiers [PDF p. 295]. His son Manuel I was a brave but reckless soldier [PDF p. 296]. Manuel's wasteful wars eventually weakened the empire's financial stability [PDF p. 297]. The dynasty ended after the tyrannical reign of Andronicus Comnenus [PDF p. 299]. The empire then fell to the incompetent Angelus brothers [PDF p. 300]. They ruled during a period when the empire was salvageable [PDF p. 300].

The text notes that the cause of Zimisces's death is uncertain [PDF p. 265]. It remains unverified if he was actually poisoned by a minister [PDF p. 265].

The Angeli dynasty presided over a declining and disorganized empire [PDF p. 301]. Isaac preferred gorgeous raiment while Alexius preferred the table [PDF p. 301]. The empire suffered from severe military and financial instability [PDF p. 301]. Isaac lost Bulgaria and Cyprus through incompetent leadership [PDF p. 303]. Alexius III later usurped the throne and blinded Isaac [PDF p. 304].

In 1203, the Fourth Crusade arrived at Venice [PDF p. 305]. The Crusaders were unable to pay their Venetian debts [PDF p. 305]. They first attacked Zara to satisfy their financial obligations [PDF p. 306]. The young Alexius Angelus promised Byzantine wealth to redirect them [PDF p. 307]. The leaders were Dandolo, Boniface, and Baldwin [PDF p. 307]. Crusaders breached the sea-walls of Constantinople using light towers [PDF p. 310]. They finally entered the city during the 1204 siege [PDF p. 314]. The Crusaders then conducted a three-day sack of the city [PDF p. 316]. They killed thousands of unarmed citizens during the plunder [PDF p. 316]. They looted churches and melted ancient statues for money [PDF p. 316, 317]. Baldwin of Flanders was elected as the new Emperor [PDF p. 318]. The conquerors partitioned the empire among themselves and Venice [PDF p. 318].

The Latin Empire faced extreme instability and territorial loss [PDF p. 320]. Baldwin I died in 1205 after being killed by Bulgarians [PDF p. 321]. Greek resistance emerged in Nicaea under Theodore Lascaris [PDF p. 324]. Theodore successfully defended his realm against the Seljouk Sultan [PDF p. 325]. Other Greek states like the Despotate of Epirus also appeared [PDF p. 326]. John III of Nicaea was an excellent and worthy heir [PDF p. 327]. Michael Paleologus eventually recaptured Constantinople in 1261 [PDF p. 331]. However, the restored empire faced severe commercial and administrative decay [PDF p. 333, 336]. Michael Paleologus's decision to disarm native militias aided the Ottomans [PDF p. 339]. This policy left the eastern frontiers vulnerable to conquest [PDF p. 339]. The Ottoman leaders Othman and Orkhan successfully expanded their domain [PDF p. 349]. Orkhan established the Janissary corps using tribute children [PDF p. 350]. This corps was the first steady infantry for an Eastern power [PDF p. 350].

The text presents differing accounts from Western and Greek chroniclers regarding the sack [PDF p. 316]. It also notes that eyewitnesses like Nicetas recorded the destruction of monuments [PDF p. 317].

The text recounts the decline of the Byzantine Empire [PDF p. 351]. John Cantacuzenus served as the prime minister under the late emperor [PDF p. 351]. He was a clever but ineffective general and statesman [PDF p. 351]. Cantacuzenus sought to imitate the rise of the Paleologi dynasty [PDF p. 351]. He called upon the Servian King Stephen Dushan for military aid [PDF p. 353]. He also utilized the assistance of Turkish princes Orkhan and Amour [PDF p. 353]. These allies helped Cantacuzenus but ultimately destroyed the Byzantine empire [PDF p. 353]. King Stephen occupied much of Macedonia and Thrace during his reign [PDF p. 353]. He even proclaimed himself the Emperor of the Servians and Romans [PDF p. 353]. Stephen Dushan died in 1355 after expanding his realm [PDF p. 354]. His young son Urosh was assassinated shortly after his death [PDF p. 354]. The empire's territory shrank significantly following these intense civil wars [PDF p. 354].

Cantacuzenus allowed Turkish horsemen to harry the local countryside [PDF p. 354]. He even gave his daughter to Orkhan in a harem [PDF p. 354]. John Paleologus ruled in conjunction with Cantacuzenus for seven years [PDF p. 354]. The empire was left with little more than the capital [PDF p. 353]. In 1354, John Paleologus attempted to reclaim his independent authority [PDF p. 355]. Cantacuzenus lost his power and was placed in a monastery [PDF p. 355]. Meanwhile, Suleiman established the first permanent Ottoman settlement at Gallipoli [PDF p. 355]. Murad I later expanded Ottoman control across much of Thrace [PDF p. 355]. The author interprets these events as the empire's gradual destruction [PDF p. 353]. Manuel II later exploited Ottoman civil wars after the Angora battle [PDF p. 361]. He recovered several territories through treaties with the Turkish pretenders [PDF p. 362]. However, Mohammed the Unifier reunited the Ottoman realm by 1421 [PDF p. 362].

Murad II later attacked the empire and forced a return to vassalage [PDF p. 365]. John VI attempted to secure Western aid through religious union [PDF p. 367]. This move at the Council of Florence caused massive Greek opposition [PDF p. 368]. Many Greeks preferred the Turkish turban to the Roman tiara [PDF p. 368]. The empire suffered from extreme exhaustion and debility during this time [PDF p. 366]. Constantinople's population had shrunk to about one hundred thousand souls [PDF p. 366]. Constantine XI eventually faced the final siege by Mohammed II [PDF p. 369]. The defenders included about three thousand Frankish soldiers and volunteers [PDF p. 370]. Ottoman artillery breached the walls of the city in 1453 [PDF p. 372]. The defense collapsed on May 29 during a massive assault [PDF p. 373]. Constantine XI perished while fighting in the breach of the walls [PDF p. 374]. Mohammed II then occupied St. Sophia and established Islamic prayer [PDF p. 375].

The section includes a table of emperors and an index [PDF p. 377, 379]. The author notes it is hard to discern why Murad I stalled [PDF p. 356].
